verses.text: Behold, a man of God came out of Judah by Yahweh’s word to Beth El; and Jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense.

He cried against the altar by Yahweh’s word, and said, “Altar! Altar! Yahweh says: ‘Behold, a son will be born to David’s house, Josiah by name. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who burn incense on you, and they will burn men’s bones on you.’”
He gave a sign the same day, saying, “This is the sign which Yahweh has spoken: Behold, the altar will be split apart, and the ashes that are on it will be poured out.”

When the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar in Bethel, Jeroboam put out his hand from the altar, saying, “Seize him!” His hand, which he put out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back again to himself.
The altar was also split apart, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by Yahweh’s word.

The king answered the man of God, “Now intercede for the favor of Yahweh your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored me again.” The man of God interceded with Yahweh, and the king’s hand was restored to him again, and became as it was before.
The king said to the man of God, “Come home with me, and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward.”
The man of God said to the king, “Even if you gave me half of your house, I would not go in with you, neither would I eat bread nor drink water in this place;
for so was it commanded me by Yahweh’s word, saying, ‘You shall eat no bread, drink no water, and don’t return by the way that you came.’”
So he went another way, and didn’t return by the way that he came to Bethel.

Now an old prophet lived in Bethel, and one of his sons came and told him all the works that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told their father the words which he had spoken to the king.
Their father said to them, “Which way did he go?” Now his sons had seen which way the man of God went, who came from Judah.
He said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” So they saddled the donkey for him; and he rode on it.
He went after the man of God, and found him sitting under an oak. He said to him, “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” He said, “I am.”
Then he said to him, “Come home with me, and eat bread.”
He said, “I may not return with you, nor go in with you. I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place.
For it was said to me by Yahweh’s word, ‘You shall eat no bread or drink water there, and don’t turn again to go by the way that you came.’”
He said to him, “I also am a prophet as you are; and an angel spoke to me by Yahweh’s word, saying, ‘Bring him back with you into your house, that he may eat bread and drink water.’” He lied to him.
So he went back with him, ate bread in his house, and drank water.
As they sat at the table, Yahweh’s word came to the prophet who brought him back;

and he cried out to the man of God who came from Judah, saying, “Yahweh says, ‘Because you have been disobedient to Yahweh’s mouth, and have not kept the commandment which Yahweh your God commanded you,
but came back, and have eaten bread and drank water in the place of which he said to you, “Eat no bread, and drink no water”; your body will not come to the tomb of your fathers.’”
After he had eaten bread, and after he drank, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back.
When he had gone, a lion met him by the way and killed him. His body was thrown on the path, and the donkey stood by it. The lion also stood by the body.
Behold, men passed by, and saw the body thrown on the path, and the lion standing by the body; and they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived.

When the prophet who brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, “It is the man of God who was disobedient to Yahweh’s mouth. Therefore Yahweh has delivered him to the lion, which has mauled him and slain him, according to Yahweh’s word, which he spoke to him.”
He said to his sons, saying, “Saddle the donkey for me,” and they saddled it.
He went and found his body thrown on the path, and the donkey and the lion standing by the body. The lion had not eaten the body, nor mauled the donkey.
The prophet took up the body of the man of God, and laid it on the donkey, and brought it back. He came to the city of the old prophet to mourn, and to bury him.
He laid his body in his own grave; and they mourned over him, saying, “Alas, my brother!”
After he had buried him, he spoke to his sons, saying, “When I am dead, bury me in the tomb in which the man of God is buried. Lay my bones beside his bones.
For the saying which he cried by Yahweh’s word against the altar in Bethel, and against all the houses of the high places which are in the cities of Samaria, will surely happen.”

After this thing Jeroboam didn’t return from his evil way, but again made priests of the high places from among all the people. Whoever wanted to, he consecrated him, that there might be priests of the high places.
This thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, even to cut it off, and to destroy it from off the surface of the earth.

footnotes.content: A man of God steps into Bethel uninvited—not a priest of Jeroboam's making, but sent by Yahweh himself. He finds the king at his own altar, burning incense to an idol. Notice the courage it took to speak when the machinery of power stood against him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophecy names Josiah—a king not yet born, who will come generations later and burn the bones of false priests on this very altar. God speaks what will be as though it already is, because He sees the whole arc. That's the kind of knowledge only the Lord possesses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sign is both a confirmation and a judgment: the altar itself will split and scatter its ashes. God doesn't just say—He proves His word by breaking the stone where the false worship happens. The tangible wreck of an altar is harder to explain away than any sermon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam reaches out to seize the prophet, but his own hand withers mid-gesture. How many times have I seen a man's will crumble the moment he tries to lay hands on God's work? The Lord's protection is sometimes a shriveled hand that teaches a king to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sign comes to pass exactly as spoken. The altar splits, the ashes pour out—a physical fact that can't be unseen, witnessed by the king and his court. When God moves, the evidence is often written in stone and ash for all to read.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam has just felt judgment fall on him, yet his first thought is to ask the prophet to pray for him. Even now, he knows who holds the real power. The prophet intercedes, and the king's hand is healed—mercy follows judgment so quickly it breaks the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After he watched his own hand wither, Jeroboam invites the man of God to dinner. He wants fellowship now—perhaps thinking gratitude and honor might sweeten the moment. But the prophet knows something about boundaries that the king doesn't yet understand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Half the kingdom—imagine the offer. And the man of God refuses it all. He's already received his orders; gold and feasts are nothing next to obedience. This is the fiber of a faithful servant: when the Lord says no, everything else becomes irrelevant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No bread, no water, don't come back the same way. The command is specific—almost strange. Perhaps the Lord knew what would tempt this man later, and built the fence ahead of time. Sometimes obedience to a small rule becomes the shield against a large falling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He goes another way—the harder road, the one nobody knows. That's always the path of someone serious about following God. It's less comfortable and more solitary, but it's the way that keeps a heart honest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An old prophet in Bethel hears the whole story—the miracles, the altar split, the withered hand restored. He's lived here long, a fixture in the town, yet he wasn't at the altar. Sometimes the people who know the most about the Lord's work are those who don't see it happening directly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old prophet asks which way the man of God went. He's tracking him now, gathering facts. The story fascinates him—or perhaps something else stirs beneath. His mind is already working toward what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saddle the donkey. A simple command, but it sets the chase in motion. The old prophet is getting ready. Some ancient hunger or curiosity or jealousy is driving him forward, though he doesn't yet know what he'll do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He finds the man of God sitting under an oak, tired perhaps, at rest. When he asks, "Are you the man of God from Judah?"—the question itself is a hook, a way in. The man answers simply: "I am." He doesn't know yet that he's about to be tested.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Come home with me, and eat bread." The old prophet speaks like a friend, like someone who simply wants to show hospitality. The invitation is soft, almost gentle. It doesn't sound like a trap, but many traps don't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man of God says no. He speaks his orders clearly: no bread, no water, no turning back the old way. He knows what he's been told. For a moment, at least, his obedience stands firm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He repeats himself—you shall eat no bread, drink no water, don't turn again. Double-speaking an order is sometimes a sign of doubt settling in. He's defending the boundary to himself now, as much as to the old prophet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I also am a prophet. An angel spoke to me." The old prophet lies—a terrible lie wearing the clothes of authority. He claims heaven sent him with a countermand. The text says plainly: "He lied to him." Sometimes the hardest tests come dressed as spiritual fellowship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He went back. Ate bread. Drank water. The obedience that stood so firm moments before crumbles in the face of a fellow prophet's word. How easily we believe someone who speaks the spiritual language, even when it contradicts what we know to be true. This is the fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As they sit at the table, Yahweh's word comes—not to the man of God, but to the old prophet who lied to him. Even in judgment, the Lord knows how to reach a heart. The word finds the old prophet in the middle of the betrayal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this strange scene: a lie dressed in spiritual language, an obedient heart swayed by authority it trusted, judgment spoken at a table where friendship is breaking. We still live in a time when false teachers speak with confidence, when counterfeit voices sound familiar, and when staying faithful to what God said—in a world that says otherwise—costs everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You have been disobedient to Yahweh's mouth." The words are measured and true. There's no ambiguity now, no room for misunderstanding. The man of God broke his command—he ate, he drank, and he came back the forbidden way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your body will not come to the tomb of your fathers." This is a grief spoken beforehand—he will die far from home, unburied with his people. It's not just death; it's a particular kind of death, spoken by the Lord himself. Obedience often carries more weight when we see what disobedience costs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After he ate and drank, he saddled the donkey for the old prophet—a small, ordinary kindness. But now he knows his fate. He's walking toward it with clear eyes, and still he does this gentle thing for the man who deceived him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A lion met him and killed him. His body lay on the path, the donkey stood by it, the lion stood by it—an eerie stillness after violence. The judgment is swift and terrible. But notice: the donkey isn't harmed, the lion doesn't eat the body. Even in judgment, there's precision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men pass by and see the strange scene: a corpse on the path, a lion standing guard, a donkey waiting. They run to tell the old prophet in the city. News travels fast when death leaves such a visible sign.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the old prophet hears, he understands at once: "It is the man of God who was disobedient. Yahweh has delivered him to the lion, according to Yahweh's word." He sees the truth now—his own lie, the man's fall, the Lord's judgment, all in one terrible moment of clarity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Saddle the donkey for me," he says again. The old prophet is going to the body—to gather it, to honor it somehow. Grief and remorse drive him now. The man he deceived is dead, and he must face what he did.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He finds the body still on the path, the donkey and the lion still standing there. The lion hasn't eaten the body, hasn't mauled the donkey. It's as if the beast itself is keeping vigil, holding the space sacred until someone comes to claim the dead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old prophet takes the body, lays it on the donkey, brings it back to his city to mourn and bury. An act of mercy toward the dead, and toward his own conscience. Sometimes the only thing left to do is honor those we've wronged by laying them to rest with care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He lays the body in his own grave. "Alas, my brother!" they cry over him. The funeral lamentation is honest grief. A stranger's body now rests in the old prophet's own tomb—a permanent marker of grief and remorse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "When I am dead, bury me beside his bones," he tells his sons. Even in death, he wants to lie beside the man he deceived. It's a strange mercy—staying near him, keeping watch, refusing to be separated even in the grave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old prophet speaks the prophecy aloud again: the saying against the altar in Bethel and all the high places will surely happen. He's bearing witness now to the truth of God's word, as if to make sure no one forgets what the man of God spoke.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But Jeroboam—he didn't turn back. The signs, the withered hand, the split altar, the death of the prophet—none of it changed his heart. Instead, he made more priests for the high places, consecrating anyone who wanted the job. Power holds tighter than truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam—even to cut it off and destroy it from the earth. A whole kingdom falls because one man refused to listen. That's the weight of it: when a leader hardens his heart, his sin reaches down through generations, like roots breaking the ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
